title: Compatibility Checking Before You Buy
description: Check whether a phone works with your accessories, carriers and ecosystem before purchase - wireless charging, eSIM, NFC, USB-C and storage.
content:
Most buyer's remorse is not about the phone — it is about the phone not working with something the buyer already owned. The headphones that will not pair, the charging pad that does not charge, the eSIM plan that will not activate. Compatibility is a set of binary checks you can run in five minutes before paying, not something to discover after unboxing.

## The accessory check

For every accessory you already own, identify the standard it uses, then find the corresponding specification field on the phone's sheet:

- **Wireless charging pads.** Check the phone lists wireless charging at all, then match the standard (Qi, Qi2) and note the wattage — a 15W phone on a 5W pad charges slowly but works; a phone without wireless charging does not work at any wattage.
- **Wired chargers.** USB-C is now near-universal on Android, but the supported charging standard varies: a proprietary fast-charging brick may fall back to slow speeds. The connector matching is the pass/fail part; the speed is a performance note.
- **Bluetooth accessories.** Any modern phone works with any modern Bluetooth headphones, but check version when range or multi-point pairing matters — older Bluetooth on the phone can limit features the headphones support.
- **Storage cards.** MicroSD support has become rare on flagships while surviving on budget models. This is a true binary: if expandable storage is not listed, no card will work.

## The carrier checks

- **SIM form factor.** Physical SIM trays versus eSIM versus dual-SIM hybrids differ by model and region. If your carrier issues eSIMs and the phone is eSIM-only in your market, a physical SIM will not help.
- **5G bands.** A phone supporting 5G generally does not mean supporting your carrier's 5G bands. Bands differ by region and carrier; if 5G matters, match the phone's listed bands against your carrier's published band list.
- **Connectivity services.** Contactless payment needs NFC and a supported wallet app; satellite messaging needs both hardware and a carrier service that offers it.

## The ecosystem checks

Ecosystem features — watch pairing, earbud fast-switching, cross-device clipboard — are usually brand-locked in practice even when the underlying standard is open. If you live in one ecosystem, verify the feature you rely on is actually offered to the other brand; documentation for these features is thinner than for hardware specs, so check the manufacturer's support pages rather than assuming.

## How to run the check

1. List the accessories and services you will not give up.
2. For each, name the standard it depends on (Qi, eSIM, microSD, NFC, a Bluetooth version).
3. Look up each standard in the phone's specification record before buying.
4. Anything missing from the sheet is unknown, not compatible-by-default — confirm with the manufacturer.

Our Compatibility Checker automates step 3 against our database: pick the phone, pick the requirement, get a documented verdict with the field value as the reason — including "not documented" when the sheet does not say. It answers specification-level compatibility only; carrier plans, regional services and third-party certifications stay outside it and should be confirmed with the relevant provider.

## The one rule

A phone that fails one of your listed checks is not automatically disqualified — but the fix (a different pad, a new plan) becomes part of its price. Count the adapter cost when comparing, and the compatibility check doubles into a true total-cost comparison.

## The five-minute pre-purchase checklist

Run these checks in order against the phone's specification page before you add anything to a cart:

1. **Charger.** Does the phone accept wired charging at a wattage your existing brick can deliver? If not, budget for a new charger — and check whether one is in the box.
2. **Wireless pad.** If you own a Qi pad, confirm the phone lists wireless charging and note the standard. A phone without the field will not charge on any pad.
3. **SIM.** Physical nano-SIM, eSIM, or both? If your carrier only issues physical SIMs and the phone is eSIM-only in your region, activation will fail.
4. **Case and screen protector.** Dimension listings (height × width × depth) predict fit; unusual camera bumps or foldable form factors often need model-specific cases that may not exist at launch.
5. **Audio.** Headphone jack presence is a hard binary. If the jack is absent, confirm your headphones are Bluetooth or USB-C and that the phone supports the codec your headphones use.

## Ecosystem checks that catch people out

- **Watch pairing.** Some smartwatches pair only with phones from the same brand or with explicit iOS/Android support listed by the watch vendor.
- **CarPlay / Android Auto.** Confirm the phone's OS version meets the head unit's minimum — older units reject newer phones less often than the reverse, but both directions exist.
- **Banking and work apps.** Rooted phones, unlocked bootloaders, and very new or very old OS versions can be rejected by security-conscious apps. Check your bank's published device requirements if you bank from the phone.
- **Accessories with app lock-in.** Earbuds, styluses and camera gimbals that depend on a companion app need that app to exist for your OS version on day one, not after an update.

## What our compatibility tool checks for you

It does not invent adapter recommendations; where a field is missing from our record, it says so rather than guessing.
